title: Seva of the mind
hook: teaching, listening and sharing knowledge kindly are seva too

segments.voice: Yesterday, daswandh, the tenth share set aside first. Your line was a tenth, for others. Did you do the math, and give a sliver? Day one hundred one.

Think of someone who taught you something small that stuck. The neighbor who showed you how to change a tire. The coworker who, on your first week, quietly explained how things really work around here. The grandparent who taught you a recipe without measuring anything. They didn't give you money. They didn't wash your dishes. They gave you something that lives in your head now, and they probably never thought of it as a gift. You've done it too. Every time you explain something patiently instead of sighing, you're giving. Sikhs have a name for that kind of giving, and it's the third of the three sevas.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SHOWED YOU HOW.` → `A GIFT THAT LIVES IN YOUR HEAD.` → `THE THIRD SEVA.`

segments.voice: Tan, dhan, and now man: the seva of the mind. Teaching what you know. Listening well. Sharing knowledge kindly, without making anyone feel small. You met a Guru who did this on day forty-five. Guru Angad took the Gurmukhi script and, tradition says, taught children to read it, so that ordinary people could read the Gurus' words for themselves. That was seva of the mind on a grand scale: knowledge handed out, not locked up. Guru Nanak says it in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: when learning is truly reflected on, it makes a person a benefactor of others. Knowledge that only makes you look clever hasn't finished its work. Knowledge that makes you useful has. There's a second half to this seva, and it's listening. In the Japji, Guru Nanak gives four whole stanzas to listening, suniai, and says that by listening, sorrow and wrongdoing are erased. Listening is how you learn. But listening to another person, really listening, is also a gift you give. Someone who feels heard has been served. And there's a word in today's hook that matters: kindly. Seva of the mind goes wrong when it turns into showing off, or correcting people so they feel stupid. The Sikh ideal is the opposite: humble, patient, glad to pass it on. Sikh communities do this in plain ways. Gurmukhi classes for children on weekends. Tutoring. Elders teaching the tunes of the hymns. Young people teaching elders how to use their phones. All of it counts. A mind can serve.
screen: `MAN — THE SEVA OF THE MIND.` · `ANGAD TEACHES CHILDREN TO READ.` · `LEARNING THAT HELPS OTHERS.` · `LISTENING IS A GIFT TOO.` · then, large: `GIVE WHAT YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you know how to do that someone near you doesn't. A shortcut on the computer. How to fold a fitted sheet. A word in another language. A way to calm down before a hard call. Now think of who could use it. Picture yourself showing them, slowly, without hurry, without making them feel slow. Notice how it feels to be patient in your imagination. That's the rehearsal. The bell holds the time.
Seva of the mind. Man seva: teaching, listening, and sharing what you know, kindly, so that others are served.
Your line: give what you know. Today, teach someone one small thing, and then listen to one person all the way to the end. Day one hundred one.

screen: `DAY 101 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHEN SEVA FEEDS THE EGO.`

howItsDone: Sikh communities run weekend Gurmukhi and kirtan classes, tutoring and study circles, and many Sikhs count teaching and patient listening as seva alongside cooking and giving.

match.prompt: what's inside the seva — tap the pairs.

myth: only work with your hands counts as seva
Sikhs count the mind's seva too: teaching, listening and sharing knowledge.
the Japji gives whole stanzas to listening
Guru Nanak gives four stanzas to suniai, listening.
seva of the mind means correcting people who are wrong
it goes wrong when it turns into showing off. the ideal is humble, patient and kind.

fork.setup: a new coworker keeps getting the same task wrong, and you know exactly how to do it. what's the seva of the mind here?
options: sigh and fix it yourself each time.
point out their mistake in the team meeting.
show them, patiently, until they've got it.
fork.reveal: seva of the mind is knowledge shared kindly. Guru Nanak says learning truly reflected on makes a person a benefactor of others.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: knowledge, learning.

trapdoor: what it means: using what you know, and how you listen, to serve other people, kindly.
what a scholar hears: man seva, completing tan, man, dhan; Guru Nanak's line that reflected learning makes one a benefactor (Ang 356), and the suniai stanzas of the Japji.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356 (Guru Nanak, Raag Asa: learning reflected on makes one a benefactor of others)
Japji Sahib, stanzas 8–11 (suniai, listening), Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2–3
Sikh tradition on Guru Angad and the Gurmukhi script

notes: Ang 356 (vidia vichari tan parupkari) paraphrased; confirm Ang and wording.
Japji stanzas 8-11 on suniai: 'sorrow and wrongdoing are erased' paraphrases the refrain (dukh pap ka nas). Confirm.
Guru Angad and Gurmukhi: tradition credits him with standardizing and teaching the script; historians debate its earlier origins. Stated as tradition; consistent with day 45.
'Third of the three sevas' refers to the order taught (hands, purse, mind), matching days 99-101.
